title: Separating readable vs. writable abort
body:
A mini-epiphany has been building these last few days. It was triggered by seeing that I'd gotten readable vs. writable abort kind of wrong (#59, #61), but also by discussions with @Raynos about how aborting a writable stream should put it into the errored state. (Currently it puts it into the "closed" state, which sucks, especially because errors in the readable stream translate to aborts on any writable streams it's piped to---you want errors.) It was also inspired by seeing how @ClaesNilsson used `abort()` in his example code in #64.

Here's the epiphany: we've been trying to treat them as if they are the same concept, even giving them the same name. _They should not be the same_.

The operation we care about _for readable streams_ is: **loss of interest in the stream and any further data**. We are signaling that we intend never to read from this stream, so please clean up any buffered data and underlying resources. Further attempts to read are programmer error, and should fail. But the stream itself did not error in any way. Call this operation "destroy," "dispose," or even "close."

The operation we care about _for writable streams_ is: **signalling that we can no longer write good data, and need to error out**. We are signaling that something went wrong acquiring data to write to the stream, and we have no intention of finishing the writing process gracefully (by calling `close()`, and letting it flush queued writes), so please throw away any queued writes and release any underlying resources. In this case, the stream itself should be put into an error state, and anyone touching it should be aware of that error. I think _this_ operation is more accurately called "abort."

When piping:
- An error in reading from the readable stream triggers an abort on the writable stream, putting the writable stream into an error state ("error propagation").
- An error writing to the writable stream (which automatically puts the writable stream into an error state) triggers a "destroy" on the readable stream, since nobody is interested in its data any more. (This could be turned off with an option to pipe, and be handled more intelligently by multi-pipe, but the base case is indeed "stop, you're done, nobody wants you anymore.")

Note that both operations are essentially synchronous: they're "stop and drop right now" operations that should immediately change the stream's state. (Although maybe if an asynchronous dispose-of-underlying-resources process fails, we should allow that to transition to an error state asynchronously, hmm. Or just let `destroy()` and `abort()` return a promise to reflect that operation, but not actually let it affect the state of the stream---that sounds better.)

---

What do you guys think? Tagging in @Raynos and @creationix because they've thought about abort and abort propagation a lot, but I think this is a big insight and it'd be great to get as much discussion as we can. I'd be especially interested in thoughts from @ClaesNilsson as he's close to the ground with TCP sockets in terms of this API.
